item.title: New AI Development Framework TRIAGE Optimizes Model Selection and Adaptation
item.description:
New AI Development Framework TRIAGE Optimizes Model Selection and Adaptation

Researchers have introduced TRIAGE, a novel framework for selecting and adapting public AI checkpoints to specific deployment scenarios. The approach addresses how organizations can effectively utilize pre-trained models without training from scratch by systematically identifying and repairing gaps between model capabilities and deployment requirements.

🧩 How it Works

TRIAGE operationalizes the selection and adaptation process through a structured five-stage pipeline:

  • Sensors and latency requirements are evaluated first with non-overridable gates
  • Local data is probed across ten minutes of operational logs
  • Model ranking occurs based on target-relevant performance among candidates passing initial gates
  • Fine-tuning proceeds with closed-loop monitoring before release
  • All stages maintain feasibility checks throughout the adaptation process

⚙️ Key Details

The framework distinguishes three distinct gap types that determine adaptation strategy:

Gap Type Repairability Description
Sensing gap Cannot be closed with sensor data Information sensors fail to capture
Latency gap Belongs to control loop, not weights Output arrives after control needs it
Distribution gap Fine-tuning can repair Mismatches between training and deployment data

Critical findings from implementation include:

  • Driving benchmarks demonstrate that latency below leading model thresholds causes 80-90% collision rates
  • Field of view loss causes 2.2-5.7x more planning errors than equivalent resolution loss
  • Local frames reduce stability gaps by 75% but increase perturbation sensitivity at limited budgets
  • Score-based selection violated gates in 2 of 4 deployment profiles tested

🚀 Availability

Real-world testing validated TRIAGE’s effectiveness:

  • Factory camera initially failed sensing gate; additional camera resolved the issue
  • Latency gate eliminated two highest-scoring candidates that couldn’t complete closed-loop trips
  • Selected model achieved acceptance in 4 of 5 closed-loop trials
  • Closed-loop validation rejected a fine-tuned model that showed offline improvement

💡 Why It Matters

TRIAGE enables organizations unable to train foundation models from scratch to:

  • Determine whether public checkpoints are compatible with their specific hardware
  • Identify necessary modifications when compatibility issues arise
  • Implement monitored adaptation processes that balance performance with safety constraints

#AI #machinelearning #modeloptimization #robotics #computervision

Source: Triage Before Fine-Tuning: Feasibility-Gated Selection and Monitored Adaptation of Embodied Foundation Models for a Fixed Physical Platform

item.title: LLM Compressor v0.14.0 adds HIGGS quantization and MXFP4xFP8 checkpoint support
item.description:
LLM Compressor v0.14.0 adds HIGGS quantization and MXFP4xFP8 checkpoint support

LLM Compressor has released version 0.14.0, introducing significant improvements to model optimization for vLLM deployment, including new quantization algorithms, pruning techniques, and support for mixed-precision formats.

🧩 How it works

The library provides comprehensive quantization and compression tools that integrate seamlessly with Hugging Face models. Key technical enhancements in v0.14.0 include:

  • HIGGS mixed-precision quantization: Collects layer-wise MSE sensitivity data and formulates an integer linear program to select an optimal mixed-precision configuration for a target average bitwidth. The resulting config can be passed to oneshot or model_free_ptq.
  • Block-wise QAD: A new QADModifier runs quantization-aware distillation after a weight-quantization modifier in the same recipe. It caches calibration inputs and the unquantized subgraph output as the teacher, then trains the quantized weights through compressed-tensors fake quantization without loading a separate teacher model.
  • Layerwise compression and sequential offloading: The sequential pipeline can decompress and compress one layer at a time, avoiding upfront whole-model conversion for large checkpoints. Onload/offload is managed manually with optional CPU staging and pinned memory.
  • Faster observers for E8M0 formats: The MSE and iMatrix observers gained exponential grid search and magnitude normalization for E8M0 scales, and the iMatrix observer now shares the MSE Triton kernel, delivering roughly 1.2-3.4x end-to-end speedups on tested models.
  • MFPTQ SpinQuant rotations: SpinQuantConverter applies offline R1/R2 Hadamard rotations directly to safetensors before model-free quantization, and model_free_ptq now accepts converter chains.
  • MoNe expert pruning: MoNe collapses low-saliency experts into constant “novice” vectors instead of removing them, keeping the router at full width while reducing expert compute.

⚙️ Key details

Several reporting and pruning features have been updated to support larger and more diverse model architectures:

  • REAP reports and non-uniform pruning: REAP now writes per-expert saliency reports, supports calibration-only report generation with sparsity=0.0, and accepts per-layer non-uniform expert sparsity. n_routed_experts is now recorded in config names, and GPT-OSS is skipped.
  • MXFP6 and MXFP4xFP8 support: Added MXFP6A8/MXFP6A16 schemes and examples, plus an MXFP4xFP8 example and refreshed quantization documentation.
  • Broader hardware and model support: The fused GPTQ Triton kernel now runs on Intel XPU, and MTP layers load through Transformers MtpModel. New checkpoints and examples include Nemotron 3.5 Super VL FP8, Zyphra Zaya1, Muse Spark, and Qwen3.6 MXFP4xFP8.
  • Docs and community: Added the Open Research Hub for community experiment results and a full Simplified Chinese README translation.

🚀 Availability

The Red Hat AI team has used LLM Compressor to produce a batch of production-ready quantized checkpoints optimized for Hopper GPUs:

Checkpoint Quantization Strategy Resulting Size
Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B Routed experts in MXFP4; attention and dense projections in FP8; ~4.2 bits per parameter ~428 GB (down from ~1644 GB)
GLM-5.3 Routed experts and dense MLPs in MXFP4; attention, shared experts, and MTP layer in FP8; ~4.5 bits per parameter ~415 GB (down from ~1507 GB)

Additional MXFP4xFP8 checkpoints are available for Qwen3.8-27B. Support for these formats in vLLM is available via PR vllm-project/vllm#64389 until it is merged.

#LLMCompressor #Quantization #vLLM #ModelOptimization #HIGGS #MXFP4

Source: vllm-project/llm-compressor

item.title: ADIndex Accelerates Token-Level Sparse Attention Indexing in Long-Context LLM Inference
item.description:
ADIndex Accelerates Token-Level Sparse Attention Indexing in Long-Context LLM Inference

ADIndex has been introduced as an adaptive and distillation-driven indexing method designed to resolve latency bottlenecks in token-level sparse attention architectures such as DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA). While DSA lowers computational costs via token-level selection, its indexer scores the entire causal prefix for each query, making indexing a primary source of latency in long-context inference.

🔍 Overview

DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) reduces the computational cost of attention by selecting tokens. However, its indexer evaluates the full causal prefix for every query, causing indexing to dominate latency during long-context workloads. At long context lengths, the indexer alone can account for more than 50% of total prefill GPU time. ADIndex addresses this computational bottleneck to make sparse attention indexing more efficient.

🧩 How it works

ADIndex incorporates three main components to optimize token-level sparse attention indexing:

  • Layer-wise calibration strategy: Adaptively accommodates cross-query retrieval overlap, motivated by observations of pronounced inter-layer heterogeneity.
  • Group-level distillation scheme: Leverages inter-layer heterogeneity to efficiently train adaptive layer-wise group indexers that capture salient retrieval signals from individual queries.
  • Low-latency inference strategy: Reduces repeated full-prefix scans by sharing token banks within query groups while retaining query-specific refinement.

⚙️ Key details

Experiments evaluating ADIndex on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.1 show significant efficiency improvements over standard DSA while preserving accuracy:

  • Task performance: Maintains near-lossless performance on LongBench, LongBench v2, and RULER benchmarks.
  • Prefill kernel speedup: Achieves up to a 6.22x speedup at a context length of 256K across layer-wise reuse configurations.
  • Decoding kernel speedup: Delivers up to a 3.40x speedup at a context length of 256K across layer-wise reuse configurations.
  • End-to-end serving speedup: Reaches a 1.54x speedup at a context length of 128K.

#ADIndex #DeepSeek #SparseAttention #LLMInference #ModelOptimization

Source: ADIndex: Layer-Adaptive Sparse Attention Indexing via Group-Level Distillation Source: TimeOmni-o1: Bidirectionally Coupling Time Series Foundation Models and LLMs for Multimodal Reasoning and Forecasting Source: One Byte, One Token: Byteifying a 27B Hybrid-Attention LLM with Self-Generated Data

item.title: LFM3 Unifies Text, Vision, Audio, Omni, and Decision Models on a 2‑Billion‑Parameter Backbone
item.description:
LFM3 Unifies Text, Vision, Audio, Omni, and Decision Models on a 2‑Billion‑Parameter Backbone

The latest release, LFM3, is the new generation of Liquid Foundation Models that unifies text, vision, audio, omni, and decision capabilities on a shared ~2 B‑parameter backbone.

🔍 Overview

  • LFM3 is built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence.
  • It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, each in the ~2 B‑parameter range.
  • Every modality model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base.

🧩 How it works

  • Tri‑hybrid architecture: 13 gated short convolutions (kernel size 7), 5 sliding‑window attention layers with a 256‑token window, and 6 global attention layers.
  • Head‑wise gated attention: a sigmoid gate scales each head’s output, allowing a head to switch off when it adds nothing.
  • Partial RoPE: global attention layers rotate only the highest‑frequency half of each head, keeping the other half invariant to distance.
  • Hardware‑in‑the‑loop architecture search redesigns the model for agentic use cases and now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs/GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Parameter efficiency: LFM3‑1.7B outperforms LFM2.5‑2.6B while using 35 % fewer parameters.
  • Speed: With an 8 K‑token context it is about 25 % faster per parameter than LFM2‑1.2B on edge devices.
  • Context window: The text model supports a 256 K‑token window; the final 3.5 T pre‑training tokens extend this window.
  • Pre‑training: 22 T tokens using the same 128 K vocabulary as LFM2.5‑8B‑A1B, with the last 3.5 T tokens emphasizing agentic traces and tool calls.
  • Edge readiness:
    • Text model fits in ~1 GB at 4‑bit precision.
    • Vision encoder combines convolution and attention, using 3× less compute than the SigLIP2 encoder in previous LFM VL models.
    • The 164 M‑parameter vision encoder matches Qwen3.5‑2B’s vision accuracy while requiring 2.2× fewer FLOPs.
    • LiquidCodec audio tokenizer turns generated tokens into speech at ~87× real‑time on a single CPU thread on Apple M4 Max and supports streaming decoding.
  • Fine‑tuning: Any modality model can be fine‑tuned on a single GPU and deployed where the application runs.

Model variants (all derived from LFM3‑1.7B‑Base)

Variant Modality Notable features
Text Text ~1 GB at 4‑bit, 256 K context window, suitable for on‑device agents
Vision Vision Convolution + attention, 3× less compute than SigLIP2, matches Qwen3.5‑2B accuracy with 2.2× fewer FLOPs
Audio Audio Uses LiquidCodec tokenizer, ~87× real‑time speech generation on Apple M4 Max, streaming decoding
Omni Omni First omni model sharing the same backbone
Decision Decision Shares backbone, optimized for agentic tasks

🚀 Availability

  • Models can be fine‑tuned on a single GPU and deployed on the target hardware, including phones, Raspberry Pi 5, laptops, cloud CPUs/GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.
  • Recommended for local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or as a base for domain‑specific fine‑tuning.

💡 Why it matters

  • The shared backbone provides more capability per parameter, allowing a 1.7 B‑parameter model to outperform larger predecessors.
  • Unified architecture across modalities reduces the need for separate model families.
  • Edge‑centric design—small size, fast inference, long context—enables advanced agentic tasks to run locally without cloud dependence.

#LiquidFoundationModels #MultimodalAI #EdgeAI #ModelOptimization

Source: Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

item.title: New Techniques Boost Efficiency of Speculative Decoding via Target Distribution Reranking
item.description:
New Techniques Boost Efficiency of Speculative Decoding via Target Distribution Reranking

Speculative decoding, which verifies drafted tokens in parallel, has been updated with two key improvements: using target‑model probability distributions to guide tree selection, and applying gated distillation during training. These changes increase acceptance rates and speed while revealing consistent shrinkage effects across many settings.

🔍 Overview

  • Speculative decoding accelerates large language models by verifying drafted tokens in parallel.
  • The method now leverages a target model’s next‑token distribution before allocating a draft tree.
  • Experiments span six target models and include both vision‑language and text‑only corpora.

🧩 How It Works

  • Tree verification: The target model checks a tree of draft tokens in parallel.
  • Distribution‑guided selection: A separately computed distribution at the current context is used to rerank first‑token branches or to draw the first token before tree allocation.
  • Training objectives: Three objectives are trained on four corpus versions:
    1. Cross‑entropy on corpus tokens.
    2. Token‑level distillation from the target.
    3. Distillation gated to positions that would survive verification.

⚙️ Key Findings

  • Reranking first‑token branches with the current‑context distribution improves expected acceptance over standard draft ranking, especially with small tree budgets.
  • Drawing the first token from this distribution before allocating the tree further improves expected acceptance, even when mean tree size is unchanged.
  • Both selection rules decode faster than draft ranking when the separate target pass overlaps standalone drafting.
  • Distillation and the verification gate provide large gains on external responses, but after greedy regeneration their impact diminishes (distillation adds a smaller gain; the gate adds little or none).
  • The observed “shrinkage” of gains persists across data orders, position weights, verifiers, decoding temperatures, and, for distillation, across initializations and learning rates.
  • Most of the shrinkage remains at the matched supervised length and at each objective’s best measured training length.
  • A second vision corpus and a text‑only replication reproduce the shrinkage, including with an autoregressive drafter.
  • Objective gains should be measured against a target‑regenerated baseline and across training lengths.

📊 Objective Effects

Objective Observed Effect
Cross‑entropy on corpus tokens Baseline training objective
Token‑level distillation from the target Large gains on external responses; smaller gain after greedy regeneration
Distillation gated to verification‑surviving positions Large gains on external responses; little or no gain after greedy regeneration; shrinkage persists across conditions

💡 Why It Matters

  • Making target probabilities available before tree allocation improves the efficiency of speculative decoding, yielding faster generation without sacrificing quality.
  • Understanding when and why gains shrink helps researchers set appropriate baselines and evaluate improvements across different training lengths and settings.
  • The findings apply to both vision‑language models and pure‑text models, indicating broad relevance.

#SpeculativeDecoding #Distillation #LanguageModels #ModelOptimization

Source: Target Regeneration Shrinks the Gains of Draft-Training Objectives in Speculative Decoding Source: Understanding Target Probability Reuse in Speculative Decoding

item.title: Compressed Active Subspaces Improve Scalability for Large Neural Network Inference
item.description:
Compressed Active Subspaces Improve Scalability for Large Neural Network Inference

Researchers have introduced Compressed Active Subspaces (CAS), a new approach designed to overcome the memory limitations of standard active subspace methods in high-dimensional models.

🔍 Overview

Active subspace methods quantify predictive uncertainty by identifying parameter directions that most significantly influence model output. While effective, traditional construction methods require storing numerous full-dimensional model gradients, which becomes impractical as model sizes grow.

🧩 How it works

CAS addresses memory constraints by utilizing a two-step process to perform inference:

  • Parameter mapping: The model parameters are mapped to a compressed space using a structured isometric embedding.
  • Subspace construction: The active subspace is constructed within this reduced parameterization.

💡 Why it matters

  • Memory efficiency: The approach substantially reduces the memory required for active subspace construction.
  • Scalability: CAS enables Bayesian inference for large models that were previously impractical to analyze.
  • Performance: Testing on neural networks of increasing size shows that CAS maintains predictive performance while providing robust uncertainty estimates.

#MachineLearning #NeuralNetworks #BayesianInference #ModelOptimization

Source: Compressed Active Subspaces for Scalable Bayesian Inference

item.title: 🚀 Kernels: The Secret Sauce Making ML Models Faster and 8-16x More Compact
item.description:
🚀 Kernels: The Secret Sauce Making ML Models Faster and 8-16x More Compact

Summary: Explore how the Kernels project slashes AI model sizes by 8-16x while improving inference speed through innovative kernel functions that eliminate computational waste. Learn why this open-source approach to quantization matters for democratizing AI deployment across diverse hardware.

🌟 Revolutionizing Model Efficiency with Kernels

Machine learning models are getting bigger, more powerful, and increasingly resource-hungry. The consequence? Deploying state-of-the-art AI has become a privilege reserved for those with access to industrial-grade hardware and infrastructure. But what if we could dramatically shrink these models while maintaining their capabilities or even making them faster?

Enter Kernels – an innovative open-source project that’s tackling the efficiency challenge head-on.

The 𝗸𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗹𝘀 project introduces a radical approach to model quantization, reducing model sizes by 8-16x while simultaneously improving inference speed. This breakthrough comes at a critical moment when the AI community is grappling with models that demand ever-increasing computational resources.

🧩 What Makes Kernels Special?

Traditional quantization approaches often face a painful tradeoff between model size and performance. The 𝙠𝙚𝙧𝙣𝙚𝙡𝙨 project takes a fundamentally different approach by reimagining how computations happen at the most fundamental level.

🔍 Kernel Functions: The Core Innovation

The magic lies in specialized kernel functions that eliminate computational redundancy. Here’s how it works:

  1. Targeted Optimization: Rather than applying generic compression techniques across the entire model, 𝗸𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗹𝘀 identifies and optimizes the most computation-intensive operations.

  2. Precision Without Waste: By carefully analyzing what precision levels are actually needed for different model components, 𝙠𝙚𝙧𝙣𝙚𝙡𝙨 applies just the right amount of precision where it matters most.

  3. Hardware Awareness: The kernel functions are designed with modern hardware architectures in mind, ensuring that the theoretical efficiency gains translate to real-world performance improvements.

🚀 Quantization with a Difference

What truly sets 𝗸𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗹𝘀 apart is how it approaches quantization:

1
2

Traditional approach: Convert all weights to lower precision uniformly
Kernels approach: Tailor precision levels based on computational impact

This tailored approach means that critical pathways in the model retain necessary precision while less sensitive areas can be dramatically compressed. The result? Models that are a fraction of their original size but maintain comparable or sometimes even improved performance characteristics.

💡 Real-world Impact and Applications

The implications of this technology extend far beyond academic interest – they fundamentally change what’s possible in practical AI deployment:

🏆 Democratizing Advanced AI

With models shrunk by 8-16x, advanced AI becomes accessible to a much wider range of devices and users. Imagine running sophisticated language models on consumer laptops or even smartphones without crushing performance issues.

⚡ Faster Inference, Lower Costs

The efficiency gains translate directly to faster inference times and significantly reduced operational costs. For large-scale deployments, this could mean:

  • Lower cloud computing bills
  • Reduced energy consumption
  • Smaller carbon footprint
  • More responsive user experiences

🌐 Edge Computing Revolution

Perhaps most exciting is how 𝙠𝙚𝙧𝙣𝙚𝙡𝙨 could accelerate the push toward edge computing. By making models compact enough to run locally on devices, we can address critical issues around privacy, latency, and connectivity constraints.

🔮 Looking Forward: The Open Source Advantage

What makes the 𝗸𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗹𝘀 project particularly promising is its open-source nature. This approach ensures:

  1. Community Improvement: The technology can evolve through contributions from researchers and practitioners worldwide.

  2. Adaptability: The methods can be applied across different model architectures and use cases.

  3. Accessibility: No proprietary barriers limit who can benefit from these advancements.

As AI continues to permeate every aspect of our digital lives, technologies like 𝙠𝙚𝙧𝙣𝙚𝙡𝙨 become increasingly crucial. They represent not just technical optimizations but a path toward more sustainable, accessible, and democratized artificial intelligence.

🤔 Final Thoughts

The 𝗸𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗹𝘀 project reminds us that innovation in AI isn’t just about creating bigger models with more parameters – it’s also about making our existing capabilities more efficient and accessible.

As we navigate the exciting but challenging frontier of AI development, approaches that prioritize efficiency without sacrificing performance will be essential. The question now becomes: How will you incorporate these quantization techniques into your own machine learning workflows to make your models lighter, faster, and more deployable?
